speechtext:
1.	Were public tenders invited by the management of the Canadian National Railways for the freighting of coal to Prince Edward Island from the mainland during the years 1924, 1925, 1926, 1927, and 1928?
2.	From what persons or firms were tenders invited, if any?
3.	Were specification and tender forms supplied? If so, what were the details?
4.	If no forms were supplied, what were the particulars and conditions?
5.	How many tenders were received in each year?
6.	What is the name of each firm or person tendering and the unit prices of each tender?
7.	Are "The Albion Lumber Company," "The New Glasgow Terminal Company" and "The Egerton Coal Company" three separate companies or are they names used by the same party for the purpose of tendering?
8.	What are the names of the president, secretary and manager of the above-named companies who have corresponded with the railways officials or signed tenders during the above years ?
9.	What amount, if any, was the railways management paid for the cargo of coal lost in transit to Prince Edward Island four years ago this season?

maintopic: QUESTIONS
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS
speechtext:
These questions have to do with the freighting of Canadian National Railway coal by water from Pictou, on the mainland, to various railway points on Prince Edward Island. The questions are designed to bring out the prices submitted for the work
referred to by numerous competitors during the last five years. The management feel that it would be unfair to all concerned to place competitors in possession of information of this kind, and hold that it is not in the public interest to give out information of that character.
Possibly it would be sufficient to say that the work in question was given wide publicity among vesselmen and forwarders on the island and adjacent shipping points, both by letter direct and by public notice by local agents of the railway; that numerous offers for the work were received, and that the lowest tenderer was given the contract.

speechtext: On t'he orders of the day:

maintopic: ATHABASKA ELECTION
subtopic: QUESTION RESPECTING MEETINGS OF PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I rise to a question of privilege in regard to inaccuracies that occur in some of the records of this house, and also in regard to the conduct of one of its standing committees. Looking over the votes and proceedings, one would be led to believe that the committee on privileges and elections bad been called for Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday of this week. Such is not the case. It was called on Tuesday, but has not been called since, and I think the necessary correction should be made in the records of the house. Further,

Athabaska Election

when we met on Tuesday, we had before us two bills, Nos. 32 and 28, which were disposed of, and thereupon the chairman immediately advised the committee that the proceedings were ended, that we had concluded the business which was before the committee. The members of the committee did not accept that, and they proceeded to consider the report of Commissioner Clarke in the Athabaska case. It was pointed out that that matter was before the committee regularly, but my recollection is that the chairman stated that that matter had been passed on last year and was not regularly before the committee. If the house will refer to the discussion which took place on Friday when the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) brought this matter up, it will be seen that on that occasion the chairman of the committee, speaking on this matter, said that the committee would be called on Tuesday, and if there was not a quorum on that day, the committee would be summoned for every subsequent day during the week. I do not know what interpretation you would put on that, but I was wondering if the interpretation was that the committee would be summoned until a quorum was obtained, and not after. I submit that we should have that committee called, and notices of the meeting sent out in the regular way, and a real effort made to have the committee meet.

maintopic: ATHABASKA ELECTION
subtopic: QUESTION RESPECTING MEETINGS OF PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext: My hon. friend spoke from a long distance, and I am not sure that I caught quite clearly everything he said. I may tell him and the members of the committee that if the committee was not convened for to-day it was because copies of a report had to be prepared. The committee has been called for next Tuesday. The order was given by me to the clerk to have the committee called for Tuesday of next week, when all the papers will be available to members of the committee.

maintopic: ATHABASKA ELECTION
subtopic: QUESTION RESPECTING MEETINGS OF PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I
feel some dissatisfaction with the explanation given by the chairman of the committee on privileges and elections. As a matter of fact, within an hour after the committee had closed its proceedings on Tuesday, I sent to the chairman twelve copies of the report of Mr. Justice Clarke, and so I do not see why there should be any delay due to the lack of copies of that report. It is now a month since this matter was debated in the House of Commons, on March 29th, and this house will [DOT]probably sit for another month, and we shall require strict attention to the business before the house if we are going to get through and to do our business in a business-like fashion. fMr. Kellner.]
There is at least one other meeting of this committee required before we can proceed to the actual business of examining witnesses. We cannot proceed very wdll without witnesses, and I think it is very unfortunate that the call that was issued for meetings of the committee both yesterday and to-day was cancelled by the chairman, because a preliminary meeting . is necessary before we can actually get down to business on the report and summon witnesses in connection with it. I think it would be better for everybody concerned if a little more enthusiasm was shown in the conduct of the business of this committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: ATHABASKA ELECTION
subtopic: QUESTION RESPECTING MEETINGS OF PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE
speechtext: This is a matter touching the privileges of this house, and I would think, Mr. Speaker, that it is not a question that can be put aside in just a light way. One of the standing committees of this house was appointed, and to that committee has been referred a definite item of business. An effort was made the other day to direct attention to the situation, and the chairman promised us that the committee would be called. A meeting was called, and then against the protest apparently of some members of the committee, it is not to meet again until next Tuesday, the meetings which were to have taken place on Wednesday and Thursday of this week having been cancelled. This committee, after all, is in the control of the house, and some steps should be taken to see that it functions in the manner in which it was intended that it should. I think the right hon. the Prime Minister will admit that any matter that touches the privileges of parliament and the conduct of public business, for which, not the Prime Minister personally, but the government as such is responsible, is worthy of being carefully considered, and every step should be taken to see that there is no deprivation of the privileges of members with respect to committees or otherwise. I feel quite sure that a word from the Prime Minister would result in the matter being put on a proper basis. If my hon. friend from Joliette (,Mr. Denis) has concluded that the duties of Chairman are too onerous or too exacting, or if he does not desire to act, I am sure he would gladly arrange that his position be taken by someone who will see that the committee meets and discharges the business for which it was appointed.

speechtext: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved the third reading of Bill No. 218, to amend the Federal District Commission Act, 1927.

maintopic: FEDERAL DISTRICT COMMISSION
subtopic: IMPROVEMENT AND BEAUTIFICATION OF OTTAWA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped that in respect to this bill the Prime Minister would have accepted the proposal of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) to limit the period during

Federal District Commission
which the annual payments are to be made to five years intead of fifteen. My chief objection to the bill is that this parliament, through a commission, is making commitments for fifteen years, which in the ordinary course of events will cover the lifetime of possibly three, if not four, parliaments. I think the principle is wrong, and I am surprised that it should be seriously proposed, especially after what the Prime Minister said in this house when in opposition and since he became head of the government. To give to a commission the expenditure of moneys over a period of fifteen years is to my mind preposterous, and to take away from future parliaments the right to say how that money shall be spent, I think is also preposterous. Therefore I move an amendment as follows, seconded by Mr. Manion:
That the bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to committee of the whole with instructions that they have power to amend by striking out the word "fifteen" in line eighteen and substituting the word "five" therefor.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: FEDERAL DISTRICT COMMISSION
subtopic: IMPROVEMENT AND BEAUTIFICATION OF OTTAWA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
in order that the house may be fully seized of the significance of the amendment, may I read that portion of the bill which it is proposed to amend? It reads as follows:
The minister is hereby authorized to pay out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada to the commission the sum of two hundred thousand dollars a year for a period not exceeding fifteen years from the first day of April, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-eight, to be expended by the commission for the purposes and subject to the provisions of this act.
As the bill was originally introduced the period was thirty years, but after listening to what was said by hon. members I agreed to amend the section by substituting fifteen years. In not accepting the further amendment of the leader of the opposition, that five years should be substituted for fifteen, I gave as the reason that this parliament at the last session did authorize the payment of $250,000 a year for sixteen years. That is the law as it stands to-day; the legislation actually in existence at the moment. The commission to-day is authorized by this parliament to receive $250,000 a year for sixteen years. Now, I have cut down from $250,000 to $200,000 the amount which this house proposes to authorize to the commission annually. I am actually proposing that the annual allowance shall be less than that to which the commission is at present entitled by way of an annual appropriation over a period of years. In those circumstances I regretted that I could not see my way to accepting the further amendment moved by the leader of the op-/Mr Chapiin.]
position, and once the house clearly understands, as it understood yesterday when it voted on the subamendment and defeated it in committee of the whole, that that law to-day does give to the commission-and it was given by hon. members on all sides at the last session-an appropriation of $250,000 for another fifteen years, while it is now proposed to give $200,000 for the same period, I hope the section will be allowed to stand as it is.

maintopic: FEDERAL DISTRICT COMMISSION
subtopic: IMPROVEMENT AND BEAUTIFICATION OF OTTAWA
speechtext: Would the commission suffer inconvenience if the amendment were passed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: FEDERAL DISTRICT COMMISSION
subtopic: IMPROVEMENT AND BEAUTIFICATION OF OTTAWA
speechtext:
I cannot say whether they would or would not. All I can say is that they have been operating this last year on the assumption that they would receive $250,000 a year, for maintenance and small local improvements, guaranteed over a period of sixteen years. I believe they have made provision with respect to the widening of driveways as well as in connection with other work to be undertaken which has to be planned years ahead if it is to be carried out successfully. This provision they have made in the expectation of the sum of $250,000 for that period of time, and I think we ought to stand by the legislation which parliament has already passed in that regard.
Broadly speaking, I agree with what is doubtless aimed at in the amendment and what in fact was stated by the leader of the opposition, that in making grants to public bodies it is well for parliament not to extend too far into the future the appropriations that are to be made annually. I would submit, however, with respect to a number of important matters which have been dealt with by this parliament in recent years, that the practice has been followed of making grants over a period of years. Grants made for technical education, for example, have been made over a period of ten years; grants made 'by hon. gentlemen opposite when in office, in aid of highway construction, were made for a period of ten years; grants made also for purposes of agricultural instruction over a period of ten years. May I say to my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) that in 1919, when his government were in office, they made a grant to this improvement commission for a period of ten years, which period was extended last year to sixteen years from 1927.
While, therefore, my hon. friend is perhaps rendering a helpful service in directing the attention of the house to the wisdom of controlling, possibly more fully than has been

Federal District Commission
the practice in the past, appropriations made by parliament, I submit with regard to this particular amendment that in the light of the legislation already enacted, the section should be permitted to stand as it is.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: FEDERAL DISTRICT COMMISSION
subtopic: IMPROVEMENT AND BEAUTIFICATION OF OTTAWA
speechtext: This particular bill is, I think, the one in which we endeavoured to apply, as something that should be observed generally in matters of this kind, the principle to which reference has been made. Personally I have held a very strong view for some considerable time as to the undesirability of any legislature or parliament tying the hauds of succeeding legislatures or parliaments with respect to annual expenditures. That idea may or may not be sound, but I do not think that when matters of policy are affected -and matters of policy always are affected in relation to grants of public moneys-this parliament should tie the hands of two or three succeeding parliaments. Not denying that parliament has always the right to repeal legislation, I submit that it is undesirable to create vested rights with respect to legislation; and the undesirability of such a policy can never be more apparent than it is in this particular measure. Last year, it is true, this house enacted a measure which granted to the commission an annuity for a period of some thirty years

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: FEDERAL DISTRICT COMMISSION
subtopic: IMPROVEMENT AND BEAUTIFICATION OF OTTAWA
speechtext: Sixteen.

maintopic: FEDERAL DISTRICT COMMISSION
subtopic: IMPROVEMENT AND BEAUTIFICATION OF OTTAWA
speechtext:
Yes, sixteen, the grant being $250,000. If my memory serves me, the matter was not challenged. The government has now introduced legislation reducmg that annual grant by $50,000, while the term of the grant is also reduced from thirty to fifteen years. As regards the reduction in the amount, that is something which must always be a matter of policy; and the government, with all the facts before it, has concluded that it is desirable to reduce the grant from a quarter of a million to $200,000 per annum. That is a matter with respect to which the government, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said, accepts fullest responsibility in the light of information obtained and of the knowledge it has of the situation in question
As to the term: the government has reduced the period of the grant from thirty to fifteen yea'rs. Our contention is merely that the very circumstances that have operated to induce the government to change its policy of last year and to reduce the grant from $250,000 to $200,000 may make it very essential for another body of men in another parliament to conclude that there should be a substantial change with respect to the whole
matter. For instance, a very strong agitation is being carried on in this city, and the Prime Minister himself admitted, not without reason -and I too am sure it is not without cause- that by reason of the government of Canada, that is to say the people collectively, owning in Ottawa some $45,000,000 of property which is not taxable, there is imposed upon the citizens a burden which is not at all commensurate with their taxing power, and that with respect to the removal of snow, the cleaning of streets, the supplying of water of proper quality, a limitation is imposed upon the ability of the city to meet the situation for the reason that it cannot tax that forty millions odd of property. The Prime Minister referred to this matter the other day. Now, it well may be that this parliament will have to make a grant in lieu of taxes to enable the city of Ottawa not to overburden its own citizens too onerously with taxes in view of the fact that there is so much government property which is exempt. That also is a matter of policy. I submit therefore that we should not do anything whereby we may bind the hands of the next parliament in its attempt to deal with this question in any way it sees fit. Grant the commission $250,000, if you like, or $300,000 or $100,000; and possibly, by reason of the circumstances that have arisen, make a contribution in lieu of taxation that might be imposed on property of the government were it not exempt. This arises out of the clear distinction which must be made, and to which the Prime Minister directed attention, between Ottawa as a municipal organization and Ottawa as the capital of Canada. Because Ottawa is the capital of the citizens of all Canada, we make this a contri-tribution towards the beautifying of the city and not for domestic municipal purposes. I cannot but think that the principle involved 

the principle which the right hon. gentleman when in opposition always contended should be applied-is the soundest possible principle with respect to the expenditure of public money. No parliament should create a condition which leaves a succeeding parliament under the necessity of either repealing existing legislation with respect to which vested interests or rights may have arisen, or of carrying on regardless of the views of that succeeding parliament, simply because the preceding government has done what is being done in this case. The cases which have been referred to, with respect to technical education, highways and matters of that kind, in my judgment, stand in exactly the same position, unless there are

Federal District Commission
very extraordinary conditions which can be submitted to parliament, and without those very extraordinary conditions, which might arise on questions touching the public debt and the necessity of liquidating it, one parliament should not say that in its wisdom it has placed upon its successors a burden which they must respect because of the interests which may have grown up under it. The power of parliament is always there, but that power cannot be always exercised efficiently because commitments may have been made and obligations created and these interests may be affected by reason of any attempt to repeal or amend such legislation.
As I say, it is with regret that one has to deal with this matter as a matter of principle with respect to this particular legislation, and I have endeavoured to assure the Prime Minister that it is because we believe a principle should be laid down which will be of very great value in this country at this time, when there is a tendency to entrust public moneys in large sums to commissions, that we are impelled by whatever sense of duty may actuate us in the discharge of our obligations here to move this amendment to the third reading of the bill.

Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey):	Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few
remarks on the main motion. It is my desire to have for the Canadian people beauty and culture. I believe that is the desire of every hon. member who sits in this house, but I do not believe that we should have splendor in the capital city while hardship exists in Canada in all too many places.
Ottawa is very well supplied with parks and driveways, and besides that it has a glorified farm not far away that serves as a park and a very beautiful one at that. If the plan as proposed by the government is carried out, the view of the parliament buildings from the driveway will be a slanting one; it will not be as good a view as could be obtained if Metcalfe street were very much widened and Wellington street were also widened. I do not think that a view from one corner would do the parliament buildings justice, because they are indeed very beautiful; and if we are going to have a driveway from which they are to be viewed by tourists and visitors, they should be viewed from the point of greatest vantage. I think that Ottawa needs very badly a good commercial hotel, a hotel which will offer to tourists and Canadians comfort and some beauty at prices they can afford to pay. I think it is true that the rank and file of the Canadian people cannot afford to stay at the Chateau Laurier. I have often noticed that the people who most frequently stay there are people who are in the enviable position of being able to pass their hotel bills on down the line.
The Canadian teachers go in parties to Washington almost every year; and I have often wondered why Canadian teachers did not come to Ottawa. It may be because they
2402	COMMONS
Federal District-Miss Macphail
cannot afford to stay in any of the hotels in which they would desire to stay. I would say that for nay own part, had I been planning this development, I would have liked to see a very good commercial hotel built on the site of the Russell house.
The Prime Minister in his very admirable speech referred to the beauty of the architecture of Greece and Rome. We all agree that their architecture is very beautiful. I have not had the privilege of seeing it but pictures lead me believe this is so. But it is known to all of us that that beauty was created by people burdened with debt and with labour. The building of some of the beautiful structures in rural England, referred to by the member for Nelson'(Mr. Bird), falls into an entirely different class. In that case the people themselves decided to build a beautiful building and taxed themselves locally, and with their own hands created the beauty. That was an expression of the ideals of the people of the community. But in this case, the expenditure proposed will bear a close resemblance to that in ancient Rome and Greece, because here the people themselves have not expressed a willingness that this money shall be spent to beautify Ottawa. The people are quite remote from Ottawa, and the most of them will never see the beauty that is Ottawa. I think Ottawa as it is is a very beautiful city. It is true, I suppose, that as time goes on its beauty will be still further enhanced.
I am not so anxious that two or three hundred years hence we will be judged by the beauty of the capital city as I am that we will, with all the facts before us, feel that we are rendering a wise decision. What we think of ourselves is much more important, in my view, than what anyone else will think of us. We live now in a social age, and so I think possibly our age will be judged by a standard different from that of the civilization of the past; I would say that the average living conditions of the individual would be a good test to apply to our civilization.
The greatest piece of art in Canada is a Canadian child; and until all Canadian children have a pretty decent chance to make something worth while of themselves, I am not going to wax very enthusiastic about making an already beautiful place more beautiful still.
There is a very interesting report which was published just recently by the Department of Health, called Maternal Mortality in Canada. I hope all the hon. members in this chamber have read that report. It contains some amazing facts, such as that in the 
fifty-ninth year of confederation 1,532 Canadian mothers died in childbirth and left motherless 5,073 children. This comment is to be found on page 26:
If these homes had been in Denmark instead of in Canada, a thousand of the mothers would not have died.
On page 27 of the report a statement has been compiled to show that the letters of advice which came from doctors who signed the death certificates of these mothers attributed death in 68 cases to the poverty of the mother. She had to go through the trial and suffering of childbirth and was too poor to be relieved of those further sufferings of which she could have been relieved if she had had more money; and 120 died from exhaustion; they went to their deaths because they had not the vitality necessary; they were overworked and under-nourished. One hundred and forty-seven of these mothers had no doctor in attendance; and it was the opinion of the doctors who wrote the letters of advice that if they had had advice the lives of many of these mothers would have been saved.
The medical profession commenting some months ago upon this report said that they had no doubt at all that 50 per cent of all these mothers could have 'been saved if the necessary measures had been taken to save them. While that is true, then, I think our first great task is this one which I have outlined.
When I think of the over-burdened farm women, of whom I know some thousands, as you who are sitting here know some other thousands-women who are very much overworked and who break down in middle life because they are overworked-my conviction is that if we are to be well thought of by succeeding generations, our first task is to make things better for Canadian mothers.
Two years ago evidence was given before the industrial committee by a certain Ontario manufacturer who stated that the wages paid in the industries in a certain town amounted to fifteen dollars a week. The Bureau of Statistics states that 8972 is the average wage paid for the whole of Canada for 1924. While these things are all true, I do not think we are justified in launching into any lavish expenditure for the beautification of an already beautiful city. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner):
That Bill No. 218 be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole with instructions to amend by striking out the words "three million dollars" in the ninth line of clause 9 and inserting therefor the words "one million seven hundred and fifty thousand dollars".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word or two on this particular question and to give the reason for my vote. I find myself in disagreement with my leader in this little group. My past experience in civic affairs is my guide in the action I take on this particular occasion. During my activities on the city council of Winnipeg, they at times went to the provincial government requesting certain grants for improvements which were more of a provincial than civic nature. Under those circumstances we were always able to obtain promises and grants as well from the provincial government of Manitoba for certain improvements in Winnipeg. If that were the case in Winnipeg and if I, as a member of the city council, could go to the provincial government and obtain grants from them for civic purposes, I cannot see how I could logically oppose a vote of this nature this afternoon, and consequently I supported the proposal of the government. I think most members of the house ought to support the government in a case of this character. We ought to have a certain amount of pride in the national capital of this Dominion and therefore we want to see a capital of such a character that we can have pride in it. Money that is spent |by the government for beautifying Ottawa is money that is well spent. I quite agree with nearly all that the previous speaker has said on this question. I am in favour of beauty and of culture. When I am in favour of beautifying the city of Ottawa, I vote in accordance with what I think; that is, I vote for and not against the grant made to beautify the city.
Another question which was brought up this afternoon was that of the control of expenditures by parliament, I am quite in agreement that parliament should have full control of all expenditures made and I do not see that by voting this sum of money this afternoon for a period of sixteen years parliament divests itself of one bit of control of the money that is going to be spent in- future years in Ottawa. Next year or any future year parliament can, if it so wishes, merely by a vote of the house, cut off its grant to the federal commission. If it so wishes it can also increase the grant which parliament has made for beautifying the city. To me the laying out of a fifteen-year project by the federal commission is equivalent to the erection of a fifteen-storey building. The plan for the whole building has to be drawn up before you start erecting it storey by storey. So when you draw up a fifteen year program for the city of Ottawa, the plans have to be laid out first so that you may know exactly what kind of a scheme you are going to go
ahead with. Therefore I can see nothing wrong in. the government asking parliament to accept such a plan.
Another question was raised by the leader of the opposition in reference to the exemption of taxation in this city. There is not in the Dominion of Canada a capital city that is not faced with exactly the same problem. In fact most cities in Canada to-day give large exemptions to corporations which are of a revenue-producing character. Parliament is not a revenue-producing institution; it exists purely for legislative and administrative purposes, and so the question of exempting from taxation the property of the government in either a national or provincial capital is on an entirely different basis from the question of exemption from taxation of commercial organizations. Therefore I do not thmk a city which is a national or provincial capital can expect to tax its government for any services it may receive from that city.
One statement, however, I should like to have had from the Prime Minister on this particular question and that is as regards the water supply of the city. I should like him to have assured the house that before any money is handed over under this legislation to the federal district commission, there would be an assurance from the civic authorities that they would take some definite steps, beyond speaking about the matter, to give to the people of Ottawa and the members who are compelled to come and reside here for several months of the year, a decent and ample supply of water. In this regard the Prime Minister might perform a good service not merely to the members but to the people of this city. This money ought not to be handed over to the commission until such assurances are given As I said before, I am in full accord with the proposals looking to the beautification of Ottawa; but I think the first essential to any city is an ample and pure supply of water, and before this money is handed over I think the Prime Minister should make some announcement to the house on this particular question. The man or woman who is well off can buy water for drinking purposes, but the poor people of the city of Ottawa are compelled to drink the water that is being supplied to them at the present time. Some members of this house have claimed that the water supply here is not fit to bathe in, and I quite agree with that sentiment. I think the Prime Minister would be doing a good service if he took this question into consideration and got some definite announcement on the matter from the city government.

Right, Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister): I did mention, when we were in committee, that I had discussed very fully with His Worship the Mayor the question of the water supply. I pointed out to him that I was perfectly sure that hon. members of this house would hesitate to vote any money for improvement purposes in the city unless they had the assurance that the city council was giving attention to the question of a pure water supply, and that they intended to deal with that matter speedily. The mayor assured me that the matter is before the city council or the board of control, and that they were hopeful that very shortly they would have a scheme evolved. I also said the other evening that if the government finds that the city does not co-operate as we hope it will, and as I know hon. members of this house expect it will, the government will move with due caution with respect to its part in the matter of co-operation.
This money is required to some extent immediately because, as hon. members know, the demolition of the buildings which have been destroyed by fire and of the property immediately adjacent cannot be postponed with advantage to anyone but with respect to other improvements I agree with my hon. friend from Winnipeg that the city ought to be given to understand that unless they do co-operate with this parliament in the matter in which we are all mutually interested, the government will ask the commission to take that fact into consideration in regard to any further allowances it may make. I might add that every expenditure made by the commission has to be authorized in the first instance by the governor in council, and speaking on behalf of the council, I would say that we will ourselves take cognizance of the city's action in this matter.
With regard to what my hon. friend the mover of the amendment (Miss Macphail) has just said, I would point out to her and to the house, that with respect to large, open spaces in the centre of cities, it is an experience the world over that those who benefit most in the end are those who, unfortunately, are in limited circumstances and who as a consequence are precluded from having the enjoyment of homes and grounds such as those more well-to-do are able to afford. Those people are unable very often to leave even their own tenements; they know nothing of a sojourn in the country over the week-end. They are the ones who perhaps more than any others derive the major benefit of the large parks in the great cities. At the rate at which development is taking place in Ot-

tawa, I am confident that it will not be long before this city will become congested in the matter of population, and I do not hesitate to say that the ones who more than any others will appreciate what this parliament is doing to-day are the mothers of little children who will find it possible to enjoy advantages for their families in this way of which otherwise they would have been deprived.

speechtext: Up to the present time what public works have been turned over to the harbour board?

speechtext:
The wharves and other
facilities constructed by the Public Works department have not yet been turned over to the harbour commission. amounts represent the expenditures made in the harbour of St. John through the agency of the Public Works department. maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: In regard to the twenty-one million dollars odd worth of property to be turned over to the commission is the government going to charge it up to the commission or make a gift of it?

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
This will be handed over
to the commission and we do not propose to make any claim in respect of interest on

St. John Harbour Commission
it. These expenditures have been made for several years past and we have never asked any interest, and they will be treated just the same now. This will be an asset to the commission; we do not intend to claim any interest.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Was not that expenditure
of $9,000,000 for Courtenay bay practically for terminals in connection with the Canadian National Railways?

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
The Canadian National

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES

The amount advanced
originally was between four and five millions. These expenditures were made in Quebec previous to 1913 through a commission different in character from the commission that has been in existence since that year. That is the reason we are charging interest, because the money was expended through the agency of a eommision while in St. John the money has been spent through the Department of Public Works.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Why charge Quebec with more responsibility than St. John?

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I am inclined to agree with my hon. friend that the port of Queber should not be discriminated against but should be given the advantage of the money spent prior to the organization of the present commission, just as we are making practically a gift to

the commission at St. John of the $21,000,000. The contention is worth considering, and in adjusting the accounts between the government and the commission I think the point should be considered in favour of the harbour at Quebec.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
The harbour of St. John is
charged with $21,000,000 already expended Is that the idea?

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES

And they will be charged
5 per cent on that expenditure?

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES

No. As I have explained,
these facilities which have been constructed through the expenditure of the $21,000,000 are to be handed over to the present commission without charge as a pure gift. This certainly will help them to obtain some return on the investment they propose to make if they are authorized to receive the loan of $5,000,000. Their liabilities will not be as great as those of Quebec.

How long has the St.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES

speechtext: Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved the second reading of Bill No. 217, to provide for a loan to the Halifax harbour commissioners.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I
wish to record my emphatic protest against the passing of this bill, because it is not in accordance with the recommendations of the * Duncan commission, which recommendations the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) a year or more ago informed the house that the government was prepared to accept practically in their entirety. I have nothing further to say now except to protest against the bill as not being in accord with the recommendations of the Duncan commission.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Marcil in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I do not rise in opposition to the expenditure of this money at the port of Halifax, particularly in view of the large sums which are being expended in other ports of Canada. Let me say first that the remarks of my hon. friend from Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston)-I am sorry he is not in his seat-have come to my notice, and when he named the commissioners who were appointed he spoke of
prominent business men of Halifax, of some considerable standing there. When he indicates to this house that they are not strong partisans and politicians, however, I take exception to his statement. The chairman of that commission, Mr. Jack, I have known for a great many years, indeed, since boyhood; we have been neighbours; as a matter of fact there is a family connection between us. His father was a very strong partisan and a constant contributor to the Liberal organ of Nova Scotia, the Halifax Chronicle. Mr. Peter Jack is a very strong partisan and an ardent worker in the Liberal interests; he is a young man of ability and energy. Mr. Ackhurst, another of the commissioners, is also a very strong partisan who works in the interests of the Liberal party on every possible occasion. The third commissioner, Mr. Murphy, has been a Liberal candidate in the constituency of Halifax, but never has been successful. I know he ran in at least one election and I believe in two, and was defeated each time. He is a constant worker. So much for the political feelings of these gentlemen. They are not, as my hon. friend said, simply Liberals; they are very ardent, earnest and hard-working Liberals.
I maintain that the Duncan report is not being carried out in connection with this vote. In Halifax we have had a very satisfactoiy system of handling the business of that port; It has been looked after with a very considerable amount of intelligence, energy and enterprise. I am sorry I have not the figures here; I asked for them, but they have not as yet reached me. I can say, however, that . as the result of the efforts of the business men of Halifax the business of that port has increased enormously in the past few years. The ship tonnage entering and clearing and the tonnage of the merchandise carried by ships coming and going have increased very considerably due to the energy and enterprise of the merchants of Halifax, and not to the appointment of any harbour commission. Halifax is situated very differently from any other port in this Dominion; it is the end of a system of railways extending across the entire country. I am repeating myself to some extent, I suppose, because I think I have touched upon these points before. But these terminals form part of the system of the Canadian National Railways. It is just as necessary for the railways of this country to have facilities with which to carry on their business as it is for any business concern to have the facilities necessary to operate successfully a private enterprise. For that reason these facilities have been under the management of the Canadian National Railways, and

Halifax Harbour Commission
as far as my knowledge goes that situation has been very satisfactory to the shipping interests of that port. Therefore we do not wish to be hampered with any commissioners; we want to be free to have the Canadian National Railways carry on this terminal work as it has been carried on in the past, unhampered by any rales or regulations which may be formulated by a commission.
So far as I know what is to be done with this vote has not appeared as yet. There are many ways in which it could be spent and in which even more money could be spent, and I am sorry a larger sum has not been granted to us. For instance, the people of Halifax are very much interested now in a bridge across the Narrows. I believe the railways are also interested in it, because at present they are operating two terminals. One is in Dartmouth, where the traffic centres from what is called the Musquodoboit railway, which is really a branch line, probably the most profitable of all branch lines of the same length in the Dominion. That has been reported to me; I do not state it as an absolute fact, but apparently it is true. At all events, a very large business is done by that road, which has a terminal in Dartmouth, across the harbour, and the traffic coming to Dartmouth has to be transferred by truck or lighter or in some other way across the harbour. This applies also to traffic coming to Halifax for Dartmouth; it has to be transported, at considerable expense, by lighter or by track. If a railway bridge were constructed between these points where traffic centres, I think the saving would be very large not only to the owners of the goods passing to and fro but to the railways as well. That is an expenditure that I would like very much to have seen provided for, at least to some extent, in the estimates.
I have pointed out the peculiar situation in connection with these terminals in that they are a part and parcel of a railway system extending over the whole Dominion and are absolutely necessary for the proper conduct of the business of that road. They were built and paid for by the railway department, and operated by it, I believe, economically and satisfactorily to the shipping interests and the public generally in Halifax. For some reason they are turned over to the Public Works department-h'ow much of them I know not, whether the wharfs only, the wharfs and elevator, the station and local freight shed there, or the whole thing. But whatever has been turned over to the Public Works, it is proposed now that a commission shall take charge of the entire business-a commission 
unacquainted with the port and with the local traffic handled by that road. Just w<hy these terminals should be turned over to the Public Works department, any more than the freight shed at any station along the road would be, is something I have not yet had explained or learned the reason for.
The traffic of the port was being carried on in a very satisfactory manner up to the time of the appointment of that commission. The commission, I believe, has not yet taken charge. I suppose up to the present they have been studying the situation; in any case thej' have made no drastic changes in the management. If there are to be charges imposed on the shipping of the port to satisfy the expenses of that commission, I for one, and the whole shipping interests and I believe the people of Halifax generally, will protest against any such tax upon the shipping of the port of Halifax. We have the credit of operating there very economically; it is perhaps the most economically managed port on the Atlantic coast, and we do not want that reputation destroyed or interfered with by any taxes upon shipping that may be imposed by this commission. Futhermore, any such tax is at present absorbed by the railway in their freight charges; that is, the freight rate covers any terminal charges there may be in connection with the traffic of that port. If the terminal charges are transferred to the shipping, then the railway benefits to that extent, and that is a situation we certainly do not want to see arise in the port oi Halifax.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I should like to say a
few words, Mr. Chairman, in regard to the subject now before the committee. I was interested in the remarks made by the hon. the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black) and in the criticism he levelled against the personnel of this commission. I took occasion the other night to express my own opinion of the personnel of the commission, to give to the house something as to the past record of these gentlemen in the business and civic life of Halifax, and to back that up by a resolution from the Halifax board of trade commending myself and the government on the selection of these commissioners, and assuring them of the board's assistance and co-operation. I do not think I ought to have to say more than that. It is down in Nova Scotia, at least, a novel and startling idea that a man is disqualified from accepting a position of this kind simply because he happens to be the adherent of a particular political party.

Halifax Harbour Commission

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
That is not the point;
it is the other qualifications.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I have tried to make it
clear what the other qualifications are, and have put on record the resolution of the board of trade.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Is it desirable to have all the members of a commission of one particular party?

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
It seemed to be on the
commission of which my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion) was a member.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
He did not stay there,
either.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
No, but his place was
taken by another who possesses the same characteristic as that spoken of by the hon. senior member for Halifax. The gentleman appointed to that commission was the one who has just resigned his position in this house, Sir Henry Drayton.
I also am a little surprised to hear the hon. senior member for Halifax suggest that the fact that a man belongs to a political party is a disqualification for a position, because I happen to remember that in the constituency of Halifax, at the last election, when I presume my hon. friend had the right to recommend, the returning officer, who is supposed to be a judicial officer, and who for years was the sheriff of the county, was displaced and the gentleman put in his place was the defeated candidate of my hon. friend's party in 1921. I should have thought that was a position in which political partisanship would not have had a part; but that was done in the very city of Halifax in which it is now suggested that adherence to a political party precludes a man from taking a position. I do not think I need take more time than to say that these gentlemen have been widely commended as having ability for the task which they have been given.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
They are only
given a half a million anyway.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
And I remember that the same party which now protests about political partisanship dismissed from office two gentlemen well and favourably known in Nova Scotia, Mr. Macdonald and Professor Rogers, efficient and qualified secretaries of the Duncan commission, because it was thought that they might have some political leanings. So that I do not think my hon. friends can claim to be so simon pure as would be suggested.
The point was raised by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) and the hon. senior member for Halifax that this legislation is not carrying out the Duncan report. That is the suggestion on the one hand; and the suggestion of the hon. senior member for Halifax, on the other hand, was that he did not want the report of the commission carried out, because he did not want the commission anyhow. I have telegrams from all over Nova Scotia asking that the Duncan commission report be carried out in every respect.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I repeat that the
appointment of the commission for the port of Halifax is not carrying out the Duncan report. The Duncan commission's report called for the nationalization of the harbour which is not being done.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
My hon. friend is suggesting that the Duncan report should not be carried out at all. The Duncan commission recommends that there shall be a statutory commission for the port of Halifax. My hon. friend (Mr. Black) is not in favour of that, notwithstanding the fact that no doubt he with hundreds of others in Nova Scotia, including representatives of boards of trade throughout the province, called on the government to implement in full the recommendations of the Duncan report. I will deal in a minute with the question which my hon. friend raises. How are we going to find out what the Duncan report means with regard to a harbour commission? The quickest way to do that would be to read the report, and my hon. friend cannot find in it one line which suggests this nebulous word "nationalization" of a port. The word is never used in the report with regard to harbour commissions. The report is made by a commission one of whom is a barrister and understands something about the English language, while another was a judge. This is the wording used in the recommendations in respect of the harbours:
We recommend that in respect of each of these two harbours the federal government should establish a statutory harbour commission, whose business it would be to see that the port facilities are developed on such a scale as will gradually-but by no means slowly-create channels through which trade can expand both winter and summer, The development of a port is as much a matter of mechanical and technical equipment, business organization and practical administration as is the development of any extensive manufacturing or industrial business.
That is the definite recommendation of the report. Again near the end of the report they state that they have been in communi-
Halifax Harbour Commission

cation with and have had a private session with-whom? With somebody who wants to put into effect new ideas about port development that have not been heard of before in Canada? No; that they have been in communication with the Montreal harbour commission, which has been established for some years; and they say after going over the operations at Montreal:
We are confirmed in our view as to what harbour commissions, (constituted of business and experienced persons) at Halifax and St. St. John could do in stimulating the trade of the maritime provinces.
And again, immediately after the reference to Montreal, they say this:
We express the hope that the recommendation we make with regard to a public commission for each of these two ports will not only be accepted but will be acted upon promptly.
The leader of the opposition the other night pointed out that something was said about railways in this part of the report. If my hon. friend will read the section carefully, he will find-and I say this with all deference -that it does not mean just exactly what he thought it did. This is what they say in the report:
We believe it is in the public interest of Canada, and in the interest of the future growth and expansion of its activities, that its Atlantic ports should be developed, just as it has been-
That means just as it has been in the interest of Canada.
-that its railways and canals should be developed-though development of these has naturally come first.
My hon. friend thought it meant that harbours should foe developed just as the railways and canals hare been developed. That is not what it says. It says that it is in the interest of Canada the Atlantic ports should be developed just as it has been in the interest of Canada that its railways and canals should be developed. Where did the idea of a statutory commission come from? When the evidence was given, were they talking about what my hon. friend referred to a few minutes ago? Let me read some of the evidence given by Mr. Cornell, the expert called before the commission by the board of trade of the city of Halifax. Mr. Cornell, as reported on page 776 of the evidence, says this:
Probably the quickest way to bring this to the attention of the commission would be to glance through the annual reports of the harbour commissions of Quebec, Montreal and Vancouver, and you will find in reading their reports that the minds of the commissioners are centred principally on the two things: Port development and solicitation of traffic; and inevitably they make a great deal of the improvement in the quantity of traffic moving through the port each year.

That is where harbour commissions are established of the kind mentioned in these bills.
We have no objection to their solicitation of traffic, and believe that they are acting wisely as trustees for that property, which belongs to the Dominion government; but we do claim, as I stated before that a similar body should be constituted

Note the words "similar body".
-for the port of Halifax and not with any idea of taking traffic away from Montreal or any other port, but rather in the hope that it will at least offset the competition of these other ports which are being developed by the aid of government money.
I am further instructed, Mr. Chairman, to place the board of trade on record that should you see fit to recommend that such an organization for the proper development of this port and the solicitation of traffic through this port be created, the endeavours of the organization to build up the port at Ilalfax will receive the utmost support of the Halifax Board of Trade.
It is as a result of those representations that the commission recommended what it did. Let me go a step further. My hon. friends seem to think that, a statutory commission having been appointed in accordance with the recommendation of the Duncan report, that is not enough. A statutory commission involves of course the financial arrangements which are generally made with regard to harbour commissions. Can anybody believe that if those gentlemen of the Duncan commission had intended the harbour commissions to be established at St. John and Halifax to be something totally different from those established at Montreal, Quebec and Vancouver, they would not have had the clearness of expression to say so? Does anybody think we would have to read whole paragraphs in order to endeavour to deduce something that was not in the words themselves? Those gentlemen, in submitting their recommendations, expressed themselves plainly and clearly. They say:	Having considered the harbour commission of Montreal, we recommend statutory commissions, and we say that having regard to the experience of Montreal those statutory commissions will benefit Halifax and St. John. I take issue with anybody who says that the government is not carrying out to the full the recommendations of the Duncan report when it establishes the harbour commissions as they are being established by these measures.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Why did the people of
Halifax, irrespective of party, oppose this commission for fully a year or more?

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
My hon. friend's question
is based on a wrong assumption. A portion of the people of Halifax worried over the

appointment of the commission. The city council were divided ten to five, I think, but that is not all the people of Halifax by any means. I think the people were a little fearful, as the hon. senior member for Halifax has said, that there might be results seriously detrimental to the port. I felt that the only thing the government could do after receiving all representations was the bold and courageous thing, namely, to go ahead and carry out the recommendations of the Duncan commission. We have already done that and what we are trying to do now is to provide the financial arrangements in connection with tho matter.
What is the benefit of a commission? It is to do away with the idea that the hon. senior member for Halifax suggested, namely, that this whole port is going to be run by the railways. I say that advisedly. My hon. friend says that, the deveiopment that was made there was made by the railway authorities. We have there railway interests, steamship interests, city interests and commercial interests, and the harbour commission is a trustee for all those interests, so to administer the port that all interests are served; that primarily there is a continuous program of development instead of having one day the board of trade suggest something, another day the railways, another day the city council and another day the people on the waterfront. The harbour commission will co-ordinate the efforts and ideas of all these interests down there in order to see that there is some continuity of administration. That is the benefit that is being received in the other ports of the Dominion and the whole question after all is one of financing.
It has been suggested that these two harbour commissions should be made advances in some different way from that adopted in the case of other harbour commissions in the Dominion of Canada. Let me remind the committee that when my hon. friend the leader of the opposition uses the words " imposing a burden " on the port of Halifax or the port of St. John, I am afraid he has not regard for the history of harbour commissions all over this country. No greater burden is intended to be imposed on these ports having regard to the service provided. The government, it seems to me, would be committing suicide and defeating the very object for which these commissions are appointed if they did something which would impose the port chaiges which would hurt the business of the port.
Mr. CANTLEY; That is what you are doing.
Halifax Harbour Commission

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: My hon. friend, may I say with all respect, does not understand the constitution or t'he working of a harbour commission.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I think I do.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I beg my hon. friend's
pardon. There is no suggestion in this bill that there shall be any increase in the port charges.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Who said there was?

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: My hon. friend the member for Pictou just a moment ago said, "That is what you are doing," and I thought that is what he meant.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I have no doubt that that is what he meant.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: That is not what he said.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: What I am arguing is that there is no suggestion in this bill at all about increasing the charges.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Of course there is not.

My hon. friend from

That is not the history of port development in Canada. The history of port development in Canada is this: What the government has done has been to receive the reports of the harbour commissioners who have been administering the ports, to examine in detail what their proposals are, and to give them, by bill, the money necessary to the carrying out of these projects for the benefit of the port; and then to ask them so far as possible to pay interest on the money advanced. But no government has ever been foolish enough to ask them to increase the tolls beyond the point which the traffic will bear or in any way to stifle or impair the business of the port. No government would be foolish enough to do that, and my hon. friend need have no fear whatever on that ground. The point is, just as in the case of the railways, that the tolls chargeable in connection with the harbour dues and port business generally are what the traffic will reasonably bear, and any government or any commission which goes beyond that and attempts to impose tolls which are too high having regard to the purpose for which the harbour is being used and the service afforded, will defeat the very objects for which the commission is established, just as the railway will defeat its object if it imposes too high charges, because it means that the traffic will not be forthcoming. That has been the history of harbour commissions up to the present.
What has been done is that the harbour commissions which have received advances have issued their bonds and have turned them over to the federal government. Those bonds represent the advances which have been made. That is, I think-and I am not prepared at this date to say it is wrong-a good way to ensure careful and prudent administration, in order that you may segregate the amount of money which has been actually advanced to the commission, in order that they may know how much money is coming from the federal treasury, and in order that the federal system of bookkeeping may be such that there will be no difficulty whatever in ear-marking particular funds going to the development of that port. Further than that this government has not gone, and further than that previous governments did not go. All they have done is to see to it that the tolls imposed have been fair.
IMr. Bennett.]
May I say one thing further? It requires the initiative of the harbour commission to fix tolls in connection with port dues and harbour charges. The commission must first recommend that the government increase the tolls. All the governmet can do is to approve or disapprove; and if the government propose to change them they have to go back to the harbour commission, and the harbour commission must concur. We can scarcely imagine men who are residents of the city of Halifax, and who have the stake in the city which I have mentioned, needlessly or improperly endeavouring to impose on shipping using the port tolls which that shipping should not bear. If the revenue from tolls fairly chargeable is not sufficient then other means will have to be found to provide the necessary money. The harbour commission may say, "We cannot pay the interest;" and I have never heard of any foreclosure proceedings against a harbour because interest has not been paid; but the issuing of these bonds has been found convenient to earmark and segregate the money which has been advanced.
So far as the financing is concerned, I think we are talking about a distinction without a difference. It seems to me that with the assurance given by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries with regard to accounting and audit, there is very little difference between one system and the other, except that under the system which now prevails you have an actual piece of paper issued bj? the harbour commission and handed over to the treasury in order that there may be a definite indication of exactly how much money has been received by the port and what expenditures have been made there by the Dominion.
The other night my hon. friend the leader of the opposition referred to the free port of Hamburg, and he suggested that the tolls at that port and at the port of London were very low because of competition. I do not expect to live long enough to see the port charges of Halifax as high as those of the free port of Hamburg. I have obtained a list of these charges, with the Canadian equivalent of the German currency, but I will not take the trouble to read the figures. I will content myself by giving the committee a description of the various dues and other charges: Quay dues on vessels, quay dues on cargo, harbour dues, delivery charges, acceptance charges, storage charges, weighing dues, crane dues, clearance fee, warehouse charges, dock labourers' wages and stevedoring. All of these tolls are charged at the port of Hamburg which has been so often referred to as a free port. I thought my hon. friend

Halifax Harbour Commission
said the other night, but I see by Hansard that I was mistaken, that this port ought to be like Hamburg

a free port. My hon. friend knows, and I presume this committee knows, that the sense in which Hamburg is a "free" port is that a certain portion-of the harbour is segregated from the rest and constitutes a sort of bonded warehouse where men may hold and store their goods and sell them without paying any duty unless they are sent into Germany. Speaking from the point of view of Halifax alone, I think it would be a very fine thing if we could have such an arrangement, but I seriously question whether it would be so regarded by the manufacturers of Canada who support my hon. friend.

I think there would be very strong objection against any suggestion that the port of Halifax or any other Canadian port be made a "free" port like Hamburg.
Fears have been expressed with respect to what may happen at the port of Halifax. The fact that only a small amount of money is being asked for this year is to me a matter of satisfaction, for it shows that the harbour commission is going slow; they are making a thorough study of the situation in an endeavour to find out what facilities can best be improved, and are determined not to ask for further advances until they know how the money should be spent to the best advantage. That is the view they have taken after a thorough investigation, and I think it will commend itself to this committee.
I do not believe there is a single port in Canada where the suggestion would be accepted to go back to the old system. We find that every port under a commission has increased its business. With all due deference to the agencies which have been at work in the port of Halifax in times past-I do not disparage their work in the slightest-I think the time has come not simply for the city of Halifax, not simply for the province of Nova Scotia, but for the benefit of the Dominion itself to take a courageous and a long view, and

if my hon. friend thinks of it in that way-to take some risks; but I do not believe there are any. In my view we should see that the two essentials emphasized by Mr. Cornell are present in the administration by the harbour commission: first, to do their utmost to provide the port with ample facilities for the business which may come to it, developed from year to year along the lines of a well-considered program; and, secondly, to do their utmost to solicit
business for the port, to bring together the man who has the goods and the man who has the ships and encourage them in the habit of trading in and out of that magnificent harbour. That is the future job of the harbour commission which has been appointed. I believe the prospects are bright, notwithstanding the fears which have been expressed by my hon. friends opposite. I join with all they have said in hoping that the charges in connection with the port will be just as low as possible. I do believe that the harbour commissioners are level-headed, sound and cautious, and at the same time courageous, and that they will endeavour to do their very utmost for the benefit of the port. If they do adjust charges, I am confident that that adjustment will be made along sound lines. In short, Mr. Chairman, I am certain that no one in this house will have reason to complain that the facilities or the business of the port have been injured by the appointment of the commission or by the legislation which has been passed, but that on the contrary my hope is that there will be a distinct advancement in keeping with the great natural advantages and the national importance of the port of Halifax.

When the committee rose at six o'clock I was dealing with the statement which has been made by the hon. the Minister of National Defence that this bill imposes no additional burden upon the trade of the port. I do not think there is any question at all as to the facts of the matter; they are that the commission has power to set such rates as they choose by by-law, they have power to pass by-laws and regulations in regard to rates. In the general act regarding the rates to be charged on the government

Halijax Harbour Commission
piers throughout the whole Dominion there appears a schedule of rates, but section 3 of that act provides:
Nothing in this act shall apply to the harbours of Toronto, Quebec, Montreal. Halifax, Pictou, or St. John, these harbours were specifically exempt from tolls.
In that connection I might say that at one time the port of Pictou was under a commission; I was a commissioner for some years on two separate occasions. The scale of fees necessary to keep the port developments in proper working order and to maintain wharves and docks was so high that trade was discouraged, and the income was not sufficient to keep up the machinery of the port. So it was decided to do away with the harbour commission, which was done on the recommendation of the commissioners themselves, as the older members of the house will no doubt remember.
Until this commission was created at Halifax the harbour dues as far as docks were concerned were absorbed by the railway: local shipments coming from the West Indies, for example and going into warehouse in the city had to pay top wharfage or side wharfage, because that material did not go over the railway. For this reason the city of Halifax, as far as its private business was concerned, did not participate in the relief afforded incoming and outgoing freight at that port. I should like to point out that Halifax harbour is the largest, the safest and the most important on the entire Atlantic coasts of this continent; as far as area is concerned, as far as safety of approach, depth of water, lighting and everything pertaining to a great harbour are concerned, Halifax has no equal on the Atlantic coast. It should be, and by nature is destined to be, the great gateway of this country of Canada. That was amply demonstrated during the war, and as I pointed out before, the difficulty in this country, and I suppose in all countries, is that as soon as the war is over we forget what our necessities were in connection with the war and minimize the importance of what is most vital to the material interests and safety of the country.
As I attempted to show before six o'clock, there is no question in my mind as to what the Duncan commission had in view and intended to express. I spent practically all one night with Sir Andrew Rae Duncan in the Halifax hotel before the report was completed, and a large portion of that time was devoted to the question of the position of the port of Halifax and how it should be developed and administered. I would not say
I am more qualified than any other man to say what was in the mind of Sir Andrew Rae Duncan in connection with this matter, but I think I am justified in stating that I know what was then his opinion and what it was he at least intended to recommend. He intended that the ports of Halifax and St. John should be developed at the national expense. I am not speaking for St. John at the moment, because except in a general way I know nothing about that port, but so far as Halifax is concerned the view taken by Sir Andrew Rae Duncan was that it should be developed at the national expense, just as the canal system of this country was developed and as the St. Lawrence waterway immediately adjacent to the ports of Quebec and Montreal were developed.

The minister made some reference to the port of Hamburg, and to a large extent he was quite correct. Hamburg is not a free port from the point of view of its being free from harbour dues. Hamburg is as we know one of the finest ports in Europe. I am fairly familiar with what the free port of Hamburg means; I have seen it and have spent some time in the free area. The minister has intimated that perhaps no man on this side of the house would be in favour of a free port at Halifax. I would. What does the "free port of Hamburg" mean? Simply this, that a very Considerable area within the port comprises a free zone into which I can take my vessel and warehouse the cargo for a considerable time. I can bring other cargoes

Halifax Harbour Commission
there from other parts of the world; I can reassort those cargoes and after thus reassorting goods from my own and other cargoes, all warehoused within the free area, make up a cargo for any port in the world, having the advantage of a warehouse where no duty is paid and from which I can reship those reassembled cargoes in various parcels. There is another phase of the free port of Hamburg, namely that goods can be taken into that port and be there reassembled and remanufactured. I am free to say that the manufacturing phase of the free port of Hamburg has not developed to the extent that was expected, and from that point of view it is not the success hoped for; but a considerable amount of remanufacturing is done in the free zone. The Minister of National Defence this afternoon delivered a carefully prepared address with respect to the situation in Halifax, With regard to the extracts which he read from Sir Andrew Rae Duncan's report I can only say that it appears to me that if he had read a little longer and a little more fully, he would not have arrived at the conclusions at which he did.
