There is a similar law with respect to the harbour of Vancouver. There is also one with respect to the harbour at Chicoutimi-or is it Bagot-ville- and there is similar legislation
Halifax Harbour Commission

with respect to the harbours of Halifax and St. John. My conclusion is that the commission meant by the Duncan report was a commission created by this parliament especially for those two harbours of Halifax and St. John. That conclusion, if it were a court of law in which one were arguing the case, is abundantly clear from the language that is employed, because Sir Andrew Duncan refers to the fact that he visited the harbour of Montreal and observed the way in which that harbour was being operated but he does not suggest in terms that the commission should be that form of commission. He says that it should be a statutory commission and then he refers to the purposes for which it was to be organized. It was to be organized, first, to administer the harbour and, second, to make the merits of the harbour known so as to develop its trade. He says at page 30 of the report:
It is not possible, within a short space of time, to make good the leeway which delayed attention has created. But we must not. on the other hand, underestimate the rapidity with which development of traffic can be expedited through the development of facilities for handling the traffic (including requisite cold storage), and through making known, by all the sources that are open to the energetic administration of harbour commissions, in the shipping exchanges of the world, and to shippers, the facilities that are offered at any given port. It would be a function of the harbour commission to survey and study the possibility of developing the export trade of the maritime provinces. In the recommendation we make as to a public commission, we do not have in mind maritime province trade standing by itself. We have also in mind the development of that trade as a factor in the development of the port, co-ordinated with the very substantial nucleus of shipping traffic that already attaches to the ports of Halifax and St. John, and co-ordinated also with the other factors which the commission's organization would influence and direct. These include the wider export (including grain shipments) and import traffic that can be organized all the year round if the full advantage is to accrue to Canada from such arrangements as lie at the foundation of their policy in regard to trade through Canadian ports, railways, trade treaties, British preference provisions, and immigration.
Those were the two fundamental principles that were in the mind of the Duncan commission as expressed in the report itself. I think it must be abundantly clear that it was never in the mind of the Duncan commission that a body should be set up which would borrow money upon which interest had to be paid and in respect to which tolls would have to be collected, but rather that the port should be developed as a national undertaking. The language I have just read is susceptible of only that conclusion; it is a burden to be placed upon the Canadian people as a whole and not upon the mere shippers of the ports

of Halifax and St. John. It points out at some length the difficulty in organizing a port and expanding its trade where there has been the delay that has characterized the ports of St. John and Halifax. If that report means anything, it means that there has been great delay in developing these ports; that is what it says in its terms.
How were these ports developed? The port of St. John was developed by money put up by the citizens of St. John plus appropriations of public money from year to year for the purpose of building breakwaters and carrying on dredging operations.

Well, a very substantial
sum was plus, and a large part of that was probably minus, as perhaps the minister will agree, so far as ultimate gain to the port itself was concerned, because tidal conditions in connection with the development of the port of St. John-and I do not know whether they will be overcome now-made it one of the most difficult ports of America in which to carry on dredging operations successfully and to build breakwaters that would withstand the enormous seas that sweep from the bay of Fundy into that harbour when certain winds prevail. But let me come to the point. What clearly must have been in the mind of the Duncan commission was that we would develop these ports in the manner I have indicated, as a national undertaking, as it says, depending not upon the traffic of the communities themselves but upon the large traffic that might be developed by a vigorous and energetic harbour commission, a body not only administering the affairs of the port but developing its trade by means such as have been employed by the harbour authorities of Liverpool or, in more recent years, the harbour authorities at Southampton, to say nothing of the development of the port of London under Lord Devonport. That was clearly in the mind of whoever wrote the report. The development of trade and the directing of the attention of the world to the facilities that exist are emphasized.
Halifax has been one of the most efficiently operated ports in America. Its piers are so located, its facilities are so good, that it can handle certain kinds of traffic faster than any other port on the continent. It is favourably located for particular kinds of traffic. There are no cranes in Halifax, as in the great ports of continental Europe for taking care of heavy traffic. The handling of that form of traffic has not yet developed in the port of Halifax, but for the purposes of a steamship of anything up to 600 or even

Halifax Harbour Commission
700 feet in length going into one of the slips at the port of Halifax, there is probably no finer harbour anywhere. It has deep water, concrete wharves, good sheds, facilities of every kind for taking care of the class of traffic other than that handled by cranes.
In St. John, owing to the abrogation of the traffic agreement with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the old government railways after 1921, when Mr. Graham declined to renew it, great impetus was given to the harbour of St. John as the "winter port of Canada, especially having regard to through traffic on. the Canadian Pacific railway. Unfortunately in many respects it became necessary for this country, because of the default of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, to take over that system, and that meant that we ourselves were developing at the harbour of Portland a port that was a rival both of St. John and of Halifax. That was one of the results of the country being compelled, by reason of the falling down of the Grand Trunk in its obligations, to take over the line that runs into Portland. Everyone knows that in Portland we have very valuable terminal facilities, costing many millions, which were built by the Grand Trunk and assisted to some extent by the community in which they are located. At one time, perhaps not since the Minister of Railways has herd that portfolio, it was thought desirable to have these sold to the state of Maine or to the city of Portland itself. But leaving that aside, the fact is that you have there a port which is a competitor of our two Canadian winter ports, one the port of Halifax and the other the port of St. John. That is one of the complaints made by the people in the maritime provinces, that Portland is a competing port of Halifax and St. John. To meet that we are going to have a statutory commission. I do not disagree entirely with what was said by the Minister of National Defence this afternoon that form seems to be the difficulty between us. We are agreed that it is to be a statutory commission, but I submit that it was a special commission that was contemplated in the report of Sir Andrew Rae Duncan. My friend the Minister of National Defence says: No, it is the ordinary commission organized under the general harbour commission law that we now have in Canada, with the same provisions that apply to the port of Vancouver or any of the other ports I have mentioned. Assume that we have a statutory commission-and my hon. friend is right when he assumes that we have; for it is a commission operating under the provisions of the general harbour commission
law; I think that is a fair way to put it. But we raise the' further point that in view of the findings made by the audit board with respect to the harbour of Quebec, that St. John harbour last year had an operating profit of $40,000 after paying interest on its investment from a gross revenue of $257,000-

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: And sinking fund too.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Yes, and taking care of
all the charges incident thereto-they had an operating profit of $39,000, to be exact, upon a gross revenue of $257,000. It is quite obvious, and here is the point upon which the Minister of National Defence and I and those associated with me disagree, that the condition that has developed at the harbour of Quebec is bound to develop at these two other ports if they carry on the trade that is so essential to competition with our own railway-owned port of Portland, and with the port of Boston and the port of New York. No man who has sailed out of St. John harbour and out of Halifax harbour into the north Atlantic in winter, and has travelled on the old Allan line out of Portland in days gone by, and who has proceeded out of the ports of Boston and New York, and has noted the vast improvements in recent years that have taken place in those American harbours, can fail for a moment to realize that if we are to develop and hold traffic for the ports of Halifax and St. John we must be able to offer facilities at least equal to those of any other port on the north Atlantic.
Now the moment you borrow $5,000,000 for the port of St. John-for it is borrowed, mark you-it involves the promise to pay; and when the Minister of National Defence says that a burden is not thereby being placed on the port, he must know that when either Halifax or St. John borrow money from the government and give a promise to pay, it assumes an obligation represented by debentures and bonds, to which are attached coupons, which are promises to pay interest. That is the point I endeavoured to make the other day. Every time, then, that the harbour commission of St. John borrows money from the Dominion government and gives its promise to pay, it has assumed an obligation, and no man would be more ready to admit that than my friend the Minister of Finance. That is the case with Quebec harbour. It has outstanding obligations, promises to pay, which for reasons that have been indicated it has not met. Halifax is to borrow $500,000 for this year. That means that the Halifax harbour commission has promised to pay $25,000 in interest to the Dominion

Halifax Harbour Commission
government, as well as sinking fund. It means more. When, three years hence, the harbour of St. John has completed its present program, it has promised to pay to the Canadian people $250,000 per annum, plus sinking fund. Now, sir, I put it to you and to every member of this house whether this is anything more than mere camouflage. If what the minister says is true, that there is no obligation to be incurred, let us say so in terms in the statute itself, and say we are granting this money to develop that harbour; let us do it direct and say we are giving, not lending, the money to develop that harbour. But, on the other hand, if we are merely swapping pieces of paper with ourselves, creating by a statute a body having power to issue promises to pay, which body will with our permission and sanction issue its promises to pay to us, which we will hold in the treasury, and when the interest comes due, and they find themselves unable to meet it, we shall have to find the money ourselves- that, it seems to me, is nothing but duplicity. It is for that reason-the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is not unmindful of it-that we appeal to the government not to put these burdens upon these ports. What is it but a burden? What is it 'but an obligation? If I exact, as a condition of my lending to my hon. friend yonder a sum of money, his promissory note, has he not assumed an obligation?

that my friend is in the fortunate position of being able to pay any promisory note he may make. But let us go a step further. I advance him $500,000 and he gives me his promissory note, with interest at 5 per cent per annum, payable say half-yearly. Will anyone say that the minister has not incurred an obligation, a liability, and that his fortune up to $500,000 is not liable for the repayment of that obligation? In this case-

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Suppose I could -not pay the interest, what would you do about it? I assure you I could not.

maintopic: LOAN OF S500.000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES

My hon. friend suggests, suppose he could not pay the annual interest. It would put him in the -position of being a defaulting debtor who might be made bankrupt; or I could put him in the position, if he had given a mortgage, of losing his property-foreclose and take the property in satisfaction of his obligation. Is that the sort of thing we want to do with these ports, hav-

ing regard to the report of the Duncan commission? I submit it is not. That is the whole story, and the whole difference between us.
Let us make -ourselves clear in this regard. On the one hand, we are all agreed that these ports must be assisted; we are all agreed that the port of St. John should have five million dollars within a period of three years to carry out the contemplated plan in connection with the first unit of its development; we are all agreed that the harbour of Halifax should have half a million dollars to take care of its present necessities as indicated by the minister for the present year. The government asks us to insist that these two ports Shall -give -us promises to pay these sums of money in a term of years, to be fixed by the government. We say that will involve, if it involves anything, the imposition of tolls for services rendered; for that is the only' way by which the respective harbour commissions could obtain revenue, unless we give them the money to pay the liability. If my friend has no money, except what his colleague the Minister of Finance gives him, with which to meet the interest charges which he owes me, or the obligations under the note that I have mentioned, the position is clear. All the harbour of Halifax and all the harbour of St. John have from which to derive their respective revenues is tservice. Each has to sell the space on the wharves- the top service, and each has the side service with respect to its berths. In addition to that it may collect certain other dues with respect to its facilities.
Mr. DUNNINlG: Grain elevators.

I thank my hon. friend:
grain elevators. Those are the services each has to sell. Now, if it. is meant seriously that they shall pay the annual interest, they can get the wherewithal to do so only by imposing charges for all the services they have to sell. I do not think that point needs to be laboured with this committee. But if on the other hand we frankly recognize that it is not intended to deal with the matter in that way, then we say: Here is the money to provide these facilities under the supervision of this parliament, under the supervision, as I said the other day,-I think the minister agrees with me-of the best expert advice that can -be given with respect to these two ports. Then we -are on common ground -and we have done the very thing which I submit is contemplated by the Duncan report.
In my opinion it is not important to consider whether this report used one word or

Halifax Harbour Commission
another. I am not attaching any particular significance to the specific use of a certain word here or there. What I am anxious about is that we Aould treat these two ports as great national ports-national in the sense of serving Canada as a whole, not the maritime provinces in particular-and by their utilization in this national way bring about that increased prosperity of the maritime provinces which their geographical position should ensure, and which is demanded in the interests of the Dominion as a whole. That is our position with respect to it.
Although the government has a sufficient majority with which to put this legislation through, I cannot think from what my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has said, that he is not fully cognizant of the difficulties of the existing situation, and I accommodate myself largely to these measures because of the observations that he has made, because of the studies that he is instituting because of the reports that he will receive, because of the expert attention which is to be given to the matter by men under his direction, and because of the undertakings that have been given with regard to checks upon the expenditures. I do not expect interest will be paid by these ports upon the advances to be made if they are to do what we want them to do. Indeed I do not wish them to pay interest if they are to do what we expect them to do, because I know that with the competition from the north Atlantic ports to the south they will not be in a position to meet the interest charges. Because of these facts, I am content to limit my opposition to these observations rather than to divide the house on a matter of this kind.

constituted of business and experienced persons.

In the appointment of the tariff commission, however, hon. gentlemen saw fit to place a defeated candidate at the head of the greatest and most important commission -a gentleman who is avowedly a candidate for the next election. He was defeated as a candidate in a constituency largely industrial, and hon. gentlemen put him at the head of a tariff commission of such importance. It seems to me that this but indicates what is in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite when dealing with this problem.
I submit that the harbour commissions of St. John and Halifax, in view of the fact that the government has accepted the Duncan commission's report, should be lifted out of party politics, and that there should be secured the services of men who are not of one political party. That is all our suggestion was. Now, my hon. friend may properly say that you cannot expect this; he may contend that it is not reasonable, human nature being what it is, inasmuch as the supporters of the government would demand that these positions be given them and them only. I pointed out however that this was the very thing that had been happening all these years in Canada and that the time had come, with this report in their hands, when the government might hope to avail themselves of the wide knowledge and experience of men on either side of politics, one of whom at least should be a Conservative and who, surely, would be able to bring to the discharge of his duties that measure of impartiality and that recognition of unity of

purpose on the part of the nation itself which would accomplish the ends contemplated in the report. Such an appointment, we contend, should be free from the taint of purely party considerations of patronage. I realize the influences that operate in such cases and I thoroughly appreciate them. I quite agree with what the minister says as to the weaknesses of human nature and the proneness of men to wish to support their own friends. And that is but a reflection of the political condition in Canada. But here you have the report of a non-political body with respect to two great harbours like St. John and Halifax, urging that they be treated somewhat differently from other ports because they belong to the people of Canada as a whole and not to the Liberal party nor to the Conservative party. That is the position we take with respect to these two harbours, about which there need be no misapprehension. Largely because of what has been stated by the Minister of Marine (Mr. Cardin) as to the position which will be occupied in the future with relation to these ports by the commissioners, we are content to express our position and avoid a recurrence of what has taken place in the past in some of the Canadian ports. If you give to St. John and Halifax the facilities necessary to meet the large increase of business which will go through those ports you will impose no extra burden upon the shipping interests. You will increase the revenuse without imposing extra fees, and in increasing the revenues you will place these ports in a position to pay interest at a proper time on the investment made by the commissions.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved the second reading of Bill No. 220, to amend the Railway Act.
He said: Perhaps if I make a short general statement as to the purport of the bill the house will accept the principle and discussion can with greater facility take place in committee.
The grade crossing fund administered by the board of railway commissioners has not been used throughout Canada to the extent which is considered by the government to be desirable. After a careful study of the reasons why this fund is not of greater use for the purpose for which is was created, the government reached the conclusion that several limitations in the existing law operated to bring about that result. One of the limitations is
56103-154J
to the effect that the fund shall not be applied to a crossing of more than four tracks. Another limits to $25,000 the maximum amount which may be granted under the existing law to any one crossing. Another limitation has to do with crossings which have come into existence since 1909, to which, under the present law, the grade crossing fund cannot be applied.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: It has not been applied?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Perhaps that would be a more correct way of putting it. The amending bill eliminates the restriction to crossings of four tracks and less, and leaves that to the discretion of the Board of Railway Commissioners. The amending bill also provides for a 40 per cent grant to be made by the Board of Railway Commissioners out of the fund with respect to crossings costing in the aggregate up to $100,000; over $100,000 in total cost the contribution from the fund may be 40 per cent, but not to exceed $100,000. By these provisions the government hopes to insure a wider use of the grade crossing fund than has been possible under the existing legislation. I have some information here with respect to the use which has been made of the fund.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: From year to year?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Not from year to year, no. The total number of crossings which have been affected by the fund since its inception in 1909 is 520. But in this connection it should be stated that with respect to 44 of the 520 the grade crossing fund has been used on two or more occasions. That will give the house an idea of the extent to which the fund has contributed to making more safe railway crossings throughout the country. I think all will agree that this result over a period of almost nineteen years is not attacking the problem as vigorously as we should desire.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: What was the total sum expended?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
From April 1, 1909, to March 31 last the total expended out of the fund was $1,368,354. I think those are all the particulars I need give at this stage. When the bill is in committee and members have before them the legislation as proposed, and on the opposite .page the legislation as it exists, it will be possible more intelligently to deal with the questions which may arise as to details. In proposing the second reading I am merely asking the house to accept the principle that the grade crossing fund should be more widely utilized. This will be rendered
Railway Act Amendment

possible by removing the limit on the number of crossings and by increasing the amount which the board may grant with respect to any individual crossing.
Mr. 'SPENCER: How much has parliament voted to this fund?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: I omitted to mention that. Parliament votes $200,000 each year under a provision in the Railway Act. This statutory provision expires in 1929. My hon. friend will notice that by the amending bill I am not proposing to extend that period. I thought it wise to get one year's experience of how the new amendments work before proposing to the house any extension of the statutory period, provided for first in 1909 for ten years, and in 1919 for an additional ten years.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: How much does the fund amount to now?

subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND

The total available under the statutory provision, including that balance, is $2,631,645. This is available for the railway commission to order grants, to be applied under the grade crossing statute.

subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND

That is made up of the
balances that would have been laid aside had you accumulated them in one fund?

subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: It is callable by the railway commission?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: The point raised by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett)- the point with which as minister I am most concerned-is the endeavour to work out something which would enable the legislation to be really effective for the purpose for which it was originally designed. There is one possible explanation as to why the grade crossing fund has not been more widely utilized by the smaller municipal communities, and that is the fact, as a reference to section 262 will show, that the principle is laid down that in connection with crossings which came into existence after 1909 the railway company assumes the whole of the responsibility except where a highway comes into existence after the railway is built. That brings about the condition that the grade crossing fund really is not made to apply in very many cases to railway crossings which came into existence after 1909. There is in the present statute, however, an exception- that the railway companies may enter into agreements with the municipality. The bill now before the committee proposes that in cases where crossings came into existence even after 1909, in the event of the railway company making an agreement with the municipality, the grade crossing fund may in future contribute towards the cost of such crossings. That is quite a broadening of the application of the fund as compared with the farmer condition referred to by the leader of the opposition. In western Canada, in the locality to which my hon. friend refers particularly, there are of course a very large number of crossings which came into existence after 1909. In fact, one might almost say that the majority of the crossings in western Canada came into existence after that date.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Not dangerous level
crossings where there are old trails.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
But in many cases new
villager have sprung up and grown into
towns since 1909, and crossings which at first were not considered by anyone to carry any considerable element of danger are now subject to increased traffic. The increase in traffic, and the change in character of the traffic, have altered completely the whole problem during the course of the years since 1909. In future, then, under the legislation now proposed, in any case in connection with crossings constructed since 1909, in which the railway company and the municipality come to any agreement, the Board of Railway Commissioners may make a contribution from the grade crossing fund. This formerly was not possible.	.
With regard to the large communities, I know the leader of the opposition will be surprised when I tell him that even under the existing statute the major contributions in the past two or three years have been to the city of Toronto, even with the $25,000 limitation and the 40 per cent limitation as well. A considerable number of grade separations have taken place in the city of Toronto during the past few years, and that city has been wise enough to take advantage of the $25,000 per crossing. Some of the municipalities have also taken advantage. of it, although not to the extent that we could desire. There is of course another reason, which hon. gentlemen representing rural communities particularly in the west will appreciate, why even with the $25,000 limitation it has not been possible for rural municipalities to avail themselves of this legislation to any considerable degree. That reason is this: that even one subway in a municipality represents, for a rural community, a very large contribution, notwithstanding that 40 per cent of the cost is borne by the grade crossing fund and another proportion by the railway itself. Add to this the further fact, to which I have referred, that crossings built since 1909 have not up to now-received any benefit from the fund, and you; will probably have an explanation as to why the fund has not 'been utilized to a greater extent.
There is another limitation to which I referred on the second reading-a limitation which it is difficult for me to understand. I refer to the four-track limitation. Even out in the country, or adjacent to villages, there are very many places where more than four tracks are involved in a very dangerous level Crossing and which at the present time could not under any circumstances benefit from the grade crossing fund. I am proposing in the bill to eliminate that four-track limitation and to leave it to the good judgment of the
Railway Act Amendment

Board of Railway Commissioners as to whether in any particular case six or eight or any number of tracks shall be considered by them.

speechtext: I rise at this stage not so much to criticize the bill as to suggest to the minister that if he is broadening the operation of the fund to the extent he indicates, then within a year or two there will be no fund left. With regard to these small rural communities, is not this fund intended to provide them with warnings like automatic bells, gates and so forth?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Then if,
within a year or so, the fund were used up and these small towns were without any supply of proper warning signals, they might find themselves in a different situation. To the various reasons given by the minister for the restricted use of the fund by western municipalities in the past, I may add that of ignorance of its being available. In my opinion most of them were not aware of the existence of the fund. The secretary of a municipality may have received a copy of the act and filed it away, and when any railway crossing problem arose no one in the council ever dreamed of such a fund as this. It could not therefore be taken advantage of. If the existence of the fund and its availability were made known to the municipalities in the constituency of my hon. friend from Macleod, or in Peace River and other places where there are crossing problems, I have no doulbt the minister would find the raids on the fund a good deal more frequent than they are at the present time. those two points together. On the second reading of the bill I mentioned that until 1909 the actual deposition of the money was carried on. There was at that time a con-

siderable accrual in the fund, and the government of the day decided that nothing more should be allowed to accumulate until the then existing fund was used. speechtext: Under the statute.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Yes. Now with reference to the point made by my hon. friend from Bow River, I think the chief reason is not so much that suggestion of ignorance to which he referred, because the railways themselves are very much alive to it. Whenever a grade crossing problem arises in any section of the country the first thing the railways do is find out whether by any chance the grade crossing fund could be made applicable. The reason is that it is limited to crossings constructed prior to 1909, and the great change which will take place is to make available the grade crossing fund to crossings constructed after 1909 but only in cases where the municipality agrees to contribute. We are not in any sense removing the responsibility which rests upon the railway in cases where the railway is junior to the highway or upon the highway where it is junior to the railway, but by this bill we are saying that if the two agree to do the job, they may get a contribution from the grade crossing fund. In that way I am hoping to make it applicable to a much larger number of the crossings which have come into existence since 1909.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
If the minister will look
into the history of this legislation I think he will find that with reference to four-track crossings the underlying idea is that when the railway occupies the space of four tracks it should look after the crossing. We have crossings over six, eight or ten tracks, and in those cases manifestly the railway should protect the crossings. When there is only a single or double track the case is a little different.
I am quite sure that is the underlying principle, and I think upon reflection the minister will agree with me. As far as the accumulation of that fund is concerned, I am afraid the difficulty is that we have not been advertising it; many sections of the country are not

Railway Act Amendment
aware that these contributions may be made.
I think there are hundreds of crossings throughout the country in connexion with which the municipalities would take advantage of that legislation if they were aware of it.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext:
There is one point which
will perhaps clarify for my hon. friend what I have in mind. There are very many crossings in the country of four tracks or more where the railway is senior to the highway; that is to say, the railway was there first, and in such a case it is a general principle of law that the highway must pay for the crossing. When the highway is there first it is a general principle of law that the railway must pay for the crossing, and in the newer sections of the country in particular there are cases in connection with rapidly extending cities or towns which are entered by country roads where crossings have been made necessary by developments which have taken place since the construction of the railway. In those cases the railways urge the old principle that he who is there first has rights which come first. It is true that the railway commission have very wide powers, and I am not laying down this principle of seniority as an absolutely fixed principle, but in general it is well known that he who is there first has rights for which he who comes second must pay if he desires to cross.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Let us finish this out.
What the minister suggests is true; in many cases the railway wtas there first, but perhaps with only a single track. Due to the growth of the town and of the railway accommodation necessary to meet that growth, the tracks have been extended to two, four, six, eight, or perhaps ten. I submit to the minister that these conditions should be met by new regulations.

Apparently the minister is
not aware of the practice of the board of railway commissioners. As far as seniority goes, when the seniority belongs to the -highway the board of railway commissioners laid down the principle long ago that this does not apply. They are inclined to apply it when the railway is senior, but where the municipality with its highway is senior you get very little comfort from the present board of railway commissioners. There is no question about that at all. As I understood it, the bill which the minister is now introducing in place of the old regulation provides that in cases of crossings which have come into existence since 1909, where there is an agreement under which
the municipality undertakes to pay a share of the cost of construction, a contribution may be made from the grade crossing fund.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext: Yes.

I think upon a little reflection the minister will see that that is not fair. A crossing which existed in 1909 later requires protection; travel either over the railway or the highway has increased so much that protection becomes necessary. It has been the policy of the railway commission for many years to be very niggardly in ordering contributions from the fund, with the result that the fund has accumulated, but of late years they have seen a little more reason and contributions have been larger and more frequent. However, this situation arises:	The road
allowance has been crossed by the railway since 1909; that road allowance may not be paved and may not be even a road. In very few cases is there an agreement between the municipality and the railway as to the future protection of that crossing when protection becomes necessary, so your bill would apply in only a very few cases. That some crossing, which has come into existence since 1909, later becomes a crossing where danger exists; the road becomes paved and travelled; the automobile traffic makes it a road which must be protected. In such a case you are going to prevent the board from making any contribution from the grade crossing fund under the terms of the bill, because it says that you can make a contribution only where there was an agreement between the railway and the municipality at the time whereby the municipality agreed to assume a share of the cost of protection.

I do not think that is
right.

That was the way the
resolution read.

speechtext:
It is not so in the bill;
the resolution was necessarily a condensation of the bill. With reference to that point I would say that in the first place I did have in mind presenting to the house the suggestion that the grade crossing fund might be made to contribute to any crossing whether it was constructed prior to 1909 or since, and I expected to meet the contention, which would have been sound, that thereby we would be relieving the railway companies of a responsibility which is now theirs under the existing law. Under the present law the railway companies are held to be responsible, subject only to these variations which have
Railway Act Amendment

to do with the question of which is senior, the highway or the railway. I thought it would' be broadening matters considerably if in connection with crossings built after 1909, wherever an agreement, say, is made now between the railway and the municipality, not having been entered into when the crossing was built, we should permit the grade crossing fund to contribute. If we broadened it to apply to all crossings I can assure the committee we would need a much larger contribution to the grade crossing fund than parliament has been making up to the present time. A statement was made as to the likelihood of the fund disappearing in a very short time as a result of these amendments. I would say in reply to that that this fund was instituted _ for the purpose of building grade crossings, and whereas parliament intended that $4,000,000 should have been expended to date in this work, as an actual fact only $1,300,000 has been expended. Parliament has been setting money aside not fot the purpose of accumulating a fund but in order to help solve the grade crossing problem, which has become more acute from year to year. Municipalities have not been taking advantage of the fund, but these provisions are designed quite frankly to bring about a spending of the money for the purposes for which the grade crosing fund was created. Perhaps the criticism is sound that the raising of the limit to $100,000 is too much. But I have had many consultations with the Board of Railway Commissioners during this year regarding the matter, and this is the outcome of a careful examination made not only by myself and the officials of the department but also by the Board of Railway Commissioners and their staff. May I remind the committee that I made that examination as the result of a debate which took place in this house last year and in the course of which complaint was made on all sides that the grade crossing fund was not being made use of. I undertook that during the recess there an examination would be made by the Department of Railways as to the reasons, and undertook to come down this session with legislation which would tend to broaden the operation of the grade crossing fund and if possible increase its use. This is the result of the undertaking I gave to the house a year ago in this regard, and it is the best thought of myself as well as of those who have been most closely connected with the administration of the law, and who are decidedly in favour of a solution of the level crossing difficulty. Important labour bodies, including the locomotive and train men, have 	j
taken a very keen interest in this legislation; they have studied it and have intimated to me that in their view a decided improvement can be brought about by the distribution of the fund under the terms of the bill now before the committee.

Clause 1 of the bill enacts

The board shall not apply any moneys out of the railway grade crossing fund towards the cost of the actual construction work, for the protection, safety and convenience of the public in respect of any existing crossing (railway crossing of a highway or highway crossing of a railway), at rail level, constructed after the first day of April, one thousand nine hundred and nine, unless and except an agreement, approved of by the board,- has been entered into between the company and a municipal or other corporation or person by which agreement the municipal or other corporation or person has agreed with the company to bear a portion of the cost of the actual construction work for the protection, safety and convenience of the public in respect of such crossing
Now the minister will see that that is exactly what I said. Suppose a crossing has come into existence since the first day of April, 1909, affecting probably not a made road but a laid out road; in not one case out. of a thousand, I have no doubt, has the railway agreed to contribute to the construction of that crossing.

subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Does my hon. friend refer to an agreement made when the railway was built?

Yes, that is my point. A
railway runs its line across a road allowance. When the time comes for the protection of that crossing, what the minister says is that at that time the municipality and the railway shall get together and make an agreement whereby the municipality agree to pay some part of the cost. If they do make an arrangement of that sort and the allocation of the cost then comes before the railway board, the board may order a contribution to the fund. But can you imagine any such case arising? By this bill a municapility may be driven into making an agreement in regard to a crossing in a case where it expects that being senior and the law being in its favour it can escape making a contribution. The minister has said that the municipality cannot receive a contribution unless it makes an agreement to contribute, while it hopes at the same time that it shall not be called upon to make a contribution.

Surely my hon. friend
has not read the existing law. Section 260, which is not affected by the present bill says:

Railway Act Amendment
In any case where a railway is constructed after the nineteenth day of May, one thousand nine hundred and nine, the company shall, at its own cost and expense, unless and except as otherwise provided by agreement, approved by the board, between the company and a municipal or other corporation or person, provide, subject to the order of the board, all protection, safety and convenience for the public in respect of any crossing of a highway by the railway.
Therefore the present law is that the onus is entirely on the railway company with respect to crossings coming into existence after 1909, but they may make an agreement with the municipality. I did not think parliament would want to get into the position of relieving the railways of any portion of that liability under section 260, but I did and I do think parliament would agree, in case a municipality deems it. important enough in its own interest to agree to pay some part of such a crossing, that the grade crossing fund might properly be asked to contribute. I fear that in answering these questions I shall come under the lash
of the leader of the opposition for posing as an authority. Least of all do I desire to pose as a legal authority in matters of this sort or, indeed, of any sort. I know a member of the legal profession is an expert in connection with all other professions and I am not a member of that distinguished body. I can answer only as a layman and, of course, as the minister responsible for the bill. I hope my hon. friend will not take any legal advice I may give him as being necessarily sound; but I would say that a letter from any municipality to the Board of Railway Commissioners would bring back definite information as to the method to be pursued, having regard to the circumstances surrunding the particular crossing-for instance, whether it came into existence before 1909 and whether the railway or the highway was there first. When I say "highway" I do not mean a constructed highway but a road allowance dedicated and set aside as a highway. All these things could be developed; but in general one might say that at the present time where a crossing has come into existence prior to 1909, the first motion on the part of a municipality would be to apply to the Board of Railway Commissioners for an order compelling the railway company to undertake the necessary grade separation or other protection. That would be the procedure prior to 1909, but I presume the municipality will have a lawyer and can get advice from someone more reliable than myself in matter of legal opinion.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: I am much obliged for the opinion. In case the railway commission decided, that some protection should be provided, what share, if any, would the municipality be called upon to contribute in regard to a crossing in existence prior to 1909? Does the act state that?

No; that is within the judgment of the Board of Railway Commissioners. I had a review made of cases that have come before the board in order to endeavour so far as I could to establish some general principle, but there was so much variation in the conditions prevailing as to make it impossible to say, as a result of that study, that a certain definite principle was applied. In general, however, the railway commission say that the cost shall be assessed against the junior party to such crossing, but this rule is subject to variation where the necessity for the protection work is largely due to the increased traffic of the senior party over the crossing. That enters into the calculation and into the judgments that have
Railway Act Amendment

been given in this regard. I take that to mean "this in a specific case: Suppose you have a road allowance in existence prior to 1009, and a railway in existence over it prior to 1909, but in 1909 the road allowance was not used at all; it was not a highway. Only recently, by reason of growth of traffic, has it become an effective source of danger. That factor is taken into account by the board in its determinations in relation to crossings in existence before 1909. It must be remembered that after 1909 section 260 governs the situation.
Mr. C'OOTE: I ask the question for this reason: There are quite a number of crossings that are really dangerous, some of them on highways to which the Dominion government has contributed. The municipalities, if they knew of the existence of this legislation and the possibility of having some contribution made, would at least foe interested in the matter, and I am endeavouring to get from the minister some information which will be of assistance to them. Could the minister tell lis-and if he cannot tell us he can say where we can get the information-what different types of protection may be erected at grade ^crossings, that is, gates and bell installations. He might also state whether these gates are automatic or whether they must have a man to operate them.

subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Subsection (4) of section 1 of this bill reads:
In this section "crossing" means any railway crossing of a highway, or any highway crossing of a railway, at rail level, and every manner of construction of the railway or of the highway by the elevation or the depression of the one above or below the other, or by the diversion of the one or the other and any other.work ordered by the board to be provided as one work of protection, safety and convenience for the public in respect of one or more railways of as many tracks crossing or so crossed as in the discretion of the board determined.
That means, first, a subway; second, a bridge; third, the elimination of a square corner which crosses the railway twice by providing a- road diversion along the railway; fourth, any other works for the protection of a railway crossing, for instance, gates, signals, and so forth.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
I am glad this question has come up in parliament this year. Level crossings constitute a tremendous problem, and if we are going to solve it by the construction of subways only, an immense amount of money and a great deal of time will be required, while tragedies will be going on in the meantime. It may be said that on the prairies the problem is not so acute because you can see a train in the distance, yet many
tragedies occur there. It is quite often the case that a man who is drifting at an angle of sixty degrees or so to a railway has his fur collar drawn up over his ears and he cannot hear or see the train coming. I have known of serious accidents occurring from that very cause. I think we should give some consideration to the means of making these crossings throughout the country safe. It might be made the subject of research by scientific men. If it is a bell that is needed, that does not cost so much, but we should find out what is the best means at the least cost. Not only are lives lost, but I understand from engineers with whom I have been in conversation that after one or two such accidents they are hardly fit for the control of their train in the future. I have been told also by conductors and engineers that quite often a motorist will hit the second or third car, because so many people do the wrong thing when suddenly faced with danger. It seems to me that either a bell or a red light or both should be installed at practically every crossing. I do not think any provincial highway should be built without providing safe crossings, or having at least some warning device. This subject might well be placed before the research council with a view to finding out the very best means of making level crossings safe, and of having this fund applied to that purpose.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
I wish to subscribe to and endorse what my hon. friend from Rose-town has said. It is a problem that we must face sooner or later in the prairie provinces at any rate. While the most of our country there is level, a very slight difference in the elevation of the land will sometimes make a great difference in visibility. Just last week there was a very serious accident at Clair, in my constituency. An automobile was struck by a Canadian National train; one woman was instantly killed, the baby died in hospital two hours later, and the man is now lying in hospital and not expected to recover. While it is open prairie country at this place, the railway track is probably seven feet above the level of the ordinary land, and the person approaching the crossing finds his view more or less obscured by box cars standing on the siding. I can quite understand, because I have travelled over that road myself, how anyone might easily miss seeing the train at the crossing. To instal even an electric bell is quite an expense and quite a problem for the ordinary rural municipality. Even the cost of upkeep of some of these devices, I presume, would be quite considerable, and where the railway winds in and out, sometimes crossing the

Railway Act Amendment
highway two or three times within a mile, it is indeed a problem. But sooner or later we must face this whole problem and try to find some appliance which will give the proper warning and be so reasonably cheap that the ordinary rural municipality can shoulder its share of the expense.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: I am thinking of an entirely different situation in British Columbia. Since 1909 both the Grand Trunk- Pacific and the Canadian Northern have been built through that province. Heretofore we have not come under the operation of the act, but now it is proposed to bring under the operation of the act, to a certain extent, the railways constructed before 1909.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Wherever an agreement exists. In the case of British Columbia the province could enter into an agreement.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Throughout the length of these railways there are no municipalities. It is all unorganizezd districts, and the province takes charge of the road work. I understand the minister to say that the province can enter into an arrangement to secure assistance from this fund?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Could recourse be had to the fund in the case of the building of new roads in these unorganized districts?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: New crossings of highways?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Yes. In my district a large program of construction is going on at the present time, with the roads paralleling and sometimes crossing the two railways I have mentioned. There may be quite a number of cases of that kind throughout the province, and I was wondering if the government of British Columbia could have recourse to the grade crossing fund in connection with crossings over these new highways.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
If there was a sharing
agreement between the authority, which in that case would be the province, and the railway, I would say yes, unquestionably. Of course, in the case mentioned by my hon. friend the highway would be junior to the railway and I could not attempt to say exactly how the board of railway commissioners would view the relationship of the province or the municipality, as the case may be, to the railway. But. it is certain that under this legislation, if an agreement came into existence, they would be able to obtain the benefit of the fund.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
The province has never
made application to get assistance from this fund?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: My hon. friend forgets that it is not in existence until we pass the bill.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: The fund has been in operation for quite a number of years, because the Canadian Pacific Railway was in operation before 1909, and all crossings on the Canadian Pacific would be entitled to the benefit of this fund.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: I have not the details before me, but looking over the five hundred odd cases I find there were cases in British Columbia. As to what authority made the application through the eighteen years, I cannot say.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: But there were applications?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Certainly, and contributions have been made with regard to crossings in British Columbia. I do not think there is a province in the Dominion that has not received some assistance from the fund during its operation.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Does the sole decision as to whether the safety device to be provided shall be a light or a bell or a subway rest with the board of railway commissioners?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
My own interpretation
of the statute-and again I speak with all deference to the lawyers present-would be that the board has the jurisdiction.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: That is the practice.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: It is the practice to submit to the judgment of the board as to the type of device to be installed.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: On the report of their engineers.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
No matter what
safety devices are provided, if it is a level crossing accidents will happen. The only safe crossing is the subway.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Or the bridge.
Mr. ROiSS (Kingston): Why not have a greater number of them provided along the old highways crossing the old Grand Trunk? Is it a matter of economy? Should not the consideration of safety be the biggest factor in the decision?
Railway Act Amendment

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: That opens up a very real and a very wide question, the whole question of providing for safety at crossings, having regard to the tremendously changed conditions in recent years with respect to vehicular traffic. So serious has the problem become in the United States that in several of the states hundreds of millions of dollars have been expended by the state in order to deal with it.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Especially in the middle west.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Especially in the states of the middle west, which are perhaps more analogous in topography to our own western country. I can assure the house that this is but a very small start on the railway crossing problem in Canada.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Like the beautification
of Ottawa.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
With reference to what my hon. friend so properly suggested just a moment ago, and also the members for Rosetown and Mackenzie, I should state this. The member for Kingston touched upon it when he said, no matter what form of protection you have, short of grade separation, you are going to have accidents. That is borne out by the fact that last year in Canada seventy-five automobiles hit the sides of moving trains-the sides; they ran into the trains instead of the trains running into them. Several of those accidents were fatal. I have not at hand information as to the number of gates that were carried away by motors, but several hundred cases occurred last year. That illustrates the point made by the member for Kingston, that so far as our present knowledge goes it appears that nothing is effective except .complete grade separation. But I do think we are making a real advance in the use of this fund as now proposed. After all, it is intended as an encouragement to the parties responsible, the railways on the one hand and the municipalities on the other, by way of contribution from the fund accumulated to develop further works of every kind by way of protection or grade separation.
But I must say that the observation of my hon. friend from Kingston conflicts with the opinion expressed by the leader of the opposition at the opening of this discussion, that it is desirable to apply the assistance of this fund to as many .crossings as possible in country districts. That protection of course in most cases takes the form of gates, lights or bells, instead of grade separation. I am

personally of the view, having regard to the experience we are having at the present time, that the more of this fund we devote to actual grade separation the better, even if as the years go by we have to ask parliament to put up a more substantial contribution in order to enable the work to be continued. In Nova Scotia and some other of the eastern provinces very valuable work is being done in the form of road diversion; that is, where the railway cuts across a winding road twice in a short distance one of the crossings is eliminated by diverting the road. This work is being studied both by the .railway engineers and the technical men of the railway commission as a means of dealing with the situation.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Occasionally the danger at a level crossing is increased by obstructing the view. I know a case where a lumber company put up a house at the corner of a very dangerous crossing. Is this covered by the bill?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
At the expense of the
crossing.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Section 258 does not say so. It gives the board power to order.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Two cases have
come to my knowledge where a coroner's jury drew the matter to the attention of somebody, but nothing was done. In one of those cases another accident has since happened.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
I think the onus would
be on the municipalities to take action; they are the bodies most intimately concerned.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Will the minister take this
into consideration? Prima facie, any crossing

Railway Act Amendment
coming into existence after 1909, as the minister has indicated, is at the expense of the railway. This proposed section is entirely in ease of the railway. If the crossing requires protection, by separation or otherwise, the 'board should order the protection and put the cost on the railway, where it belongs under section 260. Now you are tempting the railway board to resist the demand of a municipality for protection at a crossing by saying to them: We can give you a contribution towards this protection out of the grade crossing fund, but you must first go to the railway and make an agreement whereby you will assume a portion of the cost; whereas under the law you are not bound to contribute anything towards that cost.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Since we have got to
understand what was in each other's mind I have been thinking of that. The answer is simply this: There are of course cases since 1909, as I mentioned before, where,, while the highway is senior so far as dedication is concerned, yet it is in fact junior so far as use is concerned.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Trust the railway board to
get out of recognizing any seniority for a municipality.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: In such cases the railway board cannot order the municipality to pay anything under the existing law. Neither has the board power to contribute anything towards the protection of such a crossing; but the board may, and in operation frequently does, vary the general rule to the extent of not making an order against the railway company where it appears to the board that there should be some responsibility upon the municipality owing to the circumstances. I am informed that that has been the view of each succeeding chairman of the board with respect to variations which necessarily occur in the administration of this act over so wide a territory and so many thousand miles of railway.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Are any figures available to indicate whether or not accidents are more numerous at double-track than at single-track crossings? I recall a terrible accident that took place because the driver of a car containing some five or six people believed he was approaching a single-track crossing. There were two freight trains passing, one going east, the other west. He waited until the westbound train had passed and then drove his car on the track just in front of the east-bound freight. The engine of the train travelling east had blown the whistle but the two
engines were close together and in that way the accident occurred, causing the loss of three lives, I believe.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: I am not aware of any statistics which indicate a distinction between double track and single track crossings. I can inquire and let my hon. friend know.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: In provinces where municipalities have nothing to do with highways, clear of cities and towns, what is the form of co-operation?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: The province has charge.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: In all these cases where accidents have occurred and crossings are dangerous there is one outstanding difficulty: who shall make application to the railway board? The municipalities hesitate because they are under the impression that if they ask for protection the board will take the view that they should pay in proportion to the degree in which they require the protection. In my opinion there should be some automatic means by which the more dangerous crossings where accidents occur shall be taken care of. I have in mind two or three crossings in my own constituency where accidents have occurred not once but repeatedly. The municipality is afraid to go before the board for fear the board will ask it to pay more than it should. I contend that where an inquest has taken place the findings of the coroner should be forwarded to the board and some investigation automatically ensue, to determine to what extent such a crossing is dangerous and what should be done in the circumstances.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
That suggestion is in practice now; the railway commission investigates every accident of that description. But as to evolving any automatic method whereby the proportion of cost could be predetermined, without such judicial hearing as the board brings to bear, I am afraid my hon. friend is setting me a task I cannot accomplish. I do not think it would be possible. I believe the judicial hearing before the board is the only way of determining the matter. The circumstances vary so widely from one end of Canada to the other that I do not think any rule could be laid down. But it is an absurdity to presume, as some municipalities de presume, according to my hon. friend, that the board will be influenced in the amount they assess against the municipality by the fact that the municipality has applied for the crossing. I do not think there is any foundation at all for that impression. While I recognize that my hon. friend has knowledge of
Railway Act Amendment

the particular case to which he has referred. I can only assure him that there is no foundation whatever for any such idea.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: It has prevailed in two cases I know of. In one instance-the crossing at the Grand Trank Railway station going out of Oshawa-the question has been discussed for three or four years of providing a subway. The railway is endeavouring to get the municipality to make the application, and vice versa.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Do I understand the minister to say that this is available in a case where a provincial highway crosses a railway?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Yes, on the same terms as any other crossing.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: In the older provinces the old act would apply to most crossings.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: To quite a proportion.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: I have in mind a crossing on provincial highway number two in Ontario, the main highway from Toronto to Windsor, where last fall there was a serious accident. The municipality tried to get a subway and it seemed that the railway board were reluctant about granting it. Every few years there is a serious accident there. Nearly every year someone is injured and probably every three or four years someone is killed at that crossing. The crossing was straightened this year and a warning bell put in. It does seem to me that on a provincial highway, where the traffic is as great as that, some pressure should be brought to bear to have a subway provided. I know that this municipality is very much disappointed that a subway has not been secured, because the traffic is very dense on that particular highway. It is one of the most heavily travelled highways in Ontario.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Did the railway resist it?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
I could not
say.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
Will the minister
give the number of applications made, and state what has been done?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: I have given that information twice already.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
But the minister
must admit that along the Grand Trunk alone there are dozens of highways on which people are killed every summer, and nothing is done.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
I must say that this
legislation, no matter how we shape it, can-

not possibly eliminate all level crossings, and wherever there is a level crossing someone will be killed sooner or later. That is axiomatic. I cannot promise that this is any more than it purports to be, an effort to make more elastic certain provisions which have been in the law for eighteen years, and to enable money to be expended which up to now the law has not been sufficiently clastic to permit bo be spent for the purpose intended. I am not in a position as minister to discuss individual cases. I do not know the circumstances referred to by my hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Fansher), but he might himself find out, from the records in the office of the Board of Railway Commissioners, just why it was in that particular case that an order was not made. The information is public and is readily available to him. If the board set out to order a subway at every crossing in Canada where a fatal accident has occurred, they would soon break our railways. The railways could not stand the cost..

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Are all accidents-reported to the board?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
What is the use of getting
the reports unless something is done?

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext:
They investigate every
case. That is the law.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND
speechtext: Shall the section carry?

subtopic: APPLICATION OB' MONEYS FROM GRADE CROSSING FUND

Progress reported.
